name: Pali Canon
info: The Pāḷi Canon is the standard collection of scriptures of Theravada Buddhism, preserved in the Pāli language and divided into three baskets, the Tipiṭaka; it is the most complete extant early Buddhist canon.

facts.made: Held by Theravada tradition to come from the Buddha and his immediate disciples; scholars see several strata of early and late texts; derives mainly from the Tambapaṇṇiya school
facts.form: Prose and verse in Pāli, in three pitakas (baskets): Vinaya, Sutta and Abhidhamma; the Sutta Pitaka is the largest
facts.where: Palm-leaf and later manuscripts in Theravada countries, the oldest known from late in the 15th century; printed editions in Burmese, Thai, Sinhalese, Khmer and Roman script
facts.known: The Tipiṭaka or three baskets; the five nikayas of discourses; the monastic rules of the Vinaya; the seven books of the Abhidhamma; the Dhammapada; Buddhaghosa's commentaries; oral recitation and memorisation; editions at the Sixth Council

t: The Canon is the standard scripture of Theravada Buddhism, kept in Pāli and arranged in three baskets: Vinaya (monastic discipline), Sutta (discourses) and Abhidhamma (systematic doctrine).
Theravada tradition traces it to the Buddha and his early disciples, while scholars distinguish earlier and later strata and disagree about how much goes back to the Buddha himself.
It was recited orally for centuries before it was written down in Sri Lanka, and memorisation and recitation remain part of Buddhist practice.
dyk: A Burmese monk named Vicittasara learned the entire Canon by heart for the Sixth Council, according to the usual Theravada numbering.
ev: During the reign of Ashoka, an edict lists texts that correspond in part to works of the Canon, which Alexander Wynne takes as evidence that some of them were already fixed
Western scholarship suggests that the composition of the Abhidhamma Pitaka likely began around this time, perhaps drawing on earlier lists known as matrika
According to the Mahavamsa and the tradition, the Canon was written down in Sri Lanka under King Vattagamani, no earlier than 29–17 BCE by one account
The surviving Sri Lankan version was extensively redacted, about a thousand years after the Buddha's death
The Pali Text Society begins to publish its edition in Roman script, completed in 1927
The first complete printed edition of the Canon appears in Burma, in 38 volumes
The Sixth Council Tipiṭaka is published at Rangoon, in 40 volumes in Burmese script
Bhikkhu Sujato's translations of the five Nikayas are made freely available online and released into the public domain

sections.origins:
The Pāḷi Canon is the standard collection of scriptures of the Theravada Buddhist tradition, as preserved in the Pāli language. It derives mainly from the Tambapaṇṇiya school. The places named in its identifiable texts generally correspond to the Ganges region of north-eastern India, including the kingdoms of Kosala, Kasi, Vajji and Magadha.

According to Buddhist tradition, three months after the parinibbana of Gautama Buddha, a first council at Rajgir gathered his teachings: Ananda recited the Sutta Pitaka and Upali the Vinaya Pitaka, and the Arhats present accepted the recitations. The Theravada tradition states that the Canon was recited orally from the 5th century to the first century BCE, when it was written down, and holds that only a few later additions were made. Theravadins generally treat the Canon as originating with the Buddha and his immediate disciples, except for certain texts, mostly Abhidhamma, that refer to events long after his death.

Theravada tradition has generally taken Pali to be the language of Magadha as the Buddha spoke it. Linguists, however, find Pali more closely related to prakrit languages of western India, and suggest that the teachings may first have been recorded in an eastern Indian language and moved into the west Indian precursor of Pali sometime before the Asokan era.
sections.content:
The Canon falls into three pitakas, a word meaning "basket" and referring to the receptacles in which the palm-leaf manuscripts were kept; hence its traditional name, the Tipiṭaka, or "three baskets". The Vinaya Pitaka deals with the rules of the sangha, for monks and nuns. Its rules are preceded by stories of how the Buddha came to lay them down, apparently as he met behavioural problems or disputes among his followers. It has three parts: the Suttavibhanga, a commentary on the Patimokkha code; the Khandhaka, further rules grouped by topic in 22 chapters; and the Parivara, an analysis of the rules from various points of view.

The Sutta Pitaka, the largest basket, consists primarily of accounts of the Buddha's teachings and has five nikayas. The Digha Nikaya holds 34 long discourses and the Majjhima Nikaya 152 of medium length. The Samyutta Nikaya gathers thousands of short discourses in fifty-odd groups by subject or person, and the Anguttara Nikaya thousands more arranged numerically from ones to elevens. The Khuddaka Nikaya is a miscellaneous collection in prose or verse.

The Abhidhamma Pitaka offers a scholastic explanation of doctrine, particularly about mind, in seven books, among them the Dhammasangani, the Kathavatthu with over 200 debates, and the Patthana, an analysis of 24 types of condition. Traditionally abhidhamma refers to the absolute teaching, while the suttas are adapted to the hearer.
sections.making:
Views on who composed the Canon fall into several groups. Prayudh Payutto argues that it represents the Buddha's teachings essentially unchanged apart from minor modifications. Bhikkhu Sujato and Bhikkhu Brahmali hold that much of it likely dates to the Buddha's time, pointing to its technology, its political geography of India, and the absence of prophecies about King Ashoka and of places in South India.

Among academic scholars, Richard Gombrich holds that the main preachings in the Vinaya and Sutta Pitaka are coherent and must be the work of a single person, the Buddha. Peter Harvey states that much of the Canon must derive from the Buddha's teaching but that parts clearly originated after his time. Many scholars attribute the material shared with other early schools to pre-sectarian Buddhism, before those schools separated in about the fourth or third century BCE. Some scholars take an agnostic view. Ronald Davidson has little confidence that much surviving scripture is the word of the historical Buddha, and Gregory Schopen argues that definite evidence about the Canon's contents comes only in the 5th to 6th centuries CE, a position that Alexander Wynne criticised and Bhikkhu Anālayo has argued against in detail.

A majority of Western scholars regard the Vinaya, excluding the Parivāra, and the first four nikāyas as the earliest identifiable stratum. Western scholarship suggests that the Abhidhamma Pitaka began around 300 BCE, while tradition attributes it to the First Council and ascribes differences in its style to Sariputra.
sections.reception:
The Theravada describe the Canon as the Word of the Buddha (buddhavacana), though not in a literal sense, since it includes teachings by disciples. Its traditional interpretation is given in commentaries on nearly the whole Canon, compiled by Buddhaghosa (fl. 4th–5th century CE) and later monks, mainly from earlier materials now lost. Subcommentaries followed, and the tradition is summarised in Buddhaghosa's Visuddhimagga. A spokesman for the Buddha Sasana Council of Burma states that the Canon contains everything needed to show the path to nirvāna.

The Canon's earlier oral nature has not been forgotten: learning by heart and recitation remain common. Even lay people usually know a few short texts by heart, such as the Paritta, and recite them regularly, which is considered a form of meditation if the meaning is understood. The Sutta Pitaka's discourses were also shaped for audiences: Joy Manné argues that the Digha Nikaya was meant to win converts and the Majjhima Nikaya to ground them in the teaching.

The Canon's relation to Buddhism as lived is, as with other major religious traditions, problematic. The evidence suggests that only parts of it ever enjoyed wide currency, and that non-canonical works were sometimes much more widely used. Rupert Gethin suggests that the whole of Buddhist history may be regarded as a working out of the implications of the early scriptures. The Canon also uses Brahmanical terms, sometimes to link with the beliefs of Brahmins and sometimes to compare them unfavourably with Buddhist practice.
sections.survival:
The Theravada account is that the Canon was written down on palm leaves in Sri Lanka in the reign of King Vattagamani, an event later told as a "council". Scholars note that oral tradition continued beside the written texts for many centuries and that the writing was likely opposed by conservative monks. Most scholars hold that little if anything was added afterwards, though Schopen questions this. The surviving Sri Lankan version was extensively redacted in the 5th or 6th century CE, and itself mentions an earlier redaction towards the end of the 1st century BCE.

The climate of Theravada countries is not kind to manuscripts. Apart from brief quotations in inscriptions and a two-page fragment from the eighth or ninth century found in Nepal, the oldest known manuscripts date from late in the fifteenth century, and little survives from before the eighteenth. The earliest fragments of canonical Pali, from the Pyu city-states in Burma, date only to the mid-5th to mid-6th century CE.

Texts were lost when monastic ordination died out in Sri Lanka. Peter Masefield reports that records in Thailand say many texts were taken there, so that the Sri Lankan Canon was translated into Indo-Chinese Pali and in part back again. Lars Fogelin argues that the Sri Lankan Canon is a modified one, with no good reason to assume that Sri Lankan Buddhism resembles Early Buddhism on the mainland. Parallel fragments in other Indian Prakrits and Sanskrit, the Āgamas, survive mainly in Chinese.
sections.legacy:
The first complete printed edition appeared in Burma in 1900, in 38 volumes. The Pali Text Society published its Roman-script edition in 57 volumes from 1877 to 1927. A Thai edition of 45 volumes followed under Rama VII (1925–35), a Khmer one from Phnom Penh (1931–69), the Sixth Council edition at Rangoon (1954–56, 40 volumes in Burmese script) and a Sinhalese Buddha Jayanti edition of 58 volumes (from 1957). The Canon was digitised in 1996 as PALITEXT.

Translation began with the Pali Text Society's English series, from 1895, with 43 volumes so far. In 1994 its then President said most of the translations were unsatisfactory, and Paul Griffiths's term "Buddhist Hybrid English" has been applied to their style. Later translations include Bhikkhu Nanamoli and Bhikkhu Bodhi's Majjhima Nikaya (1995), Bodhi's Samyutta (2003) and Anguttara (2012), and Bhikkhu Sujato's five Nikayas of 2018, in the public domain. A Japanese translation in 65 volumes was published from 1935 to 1941.

The Canon stands beside two other main canons, the Chinese Buddhist Canon and the Tibetan Kangyur. These are not translations of the Pali but contain some recognisably similar early works, and their Abhidharma books are fundamentally different from the Pali Abhidhamma Pitaka. The Pali Canon, the most complete extant early Buddhist canon, remains the scriptural basis of Theravada practice.

summary: The Pāḷi Canon is the Theravada Buddhist scripture in Pāli, arranged in three baskets of discipline, discourses and systematic doctrine. Tradition traces it to the Buddha and his disciples; scholars disagree on how much does, and it was written down in Sri Lanka.
references: Oskar von Hinüber, A Handbook of Pāli Literature (Walter de Gruyter, 2000)
Rupert Gethin, Foundations of Buddhism (Oxford University Press, 1998)
Peter Harvey, Introduction to Buddhism (Cambridge University Press, 1990)
notes: start -300 (circa) is my choice: the article gives no date for the oldest text. It gives c. 300 BCE for the beginning of the Abhidhamma (the latest part), the Ashoka reign 304-232 BC for texts already fixed, and 29 BC for writing down. The editor may prefer another start.
The article gives the writing down as 29 BC at the Fourth Council in one place and 'no earlier than 29-17 BC' at the Alu Viharaya Temple in another; the event list uses 29 BCE with the hedge.
The article says oral recitation 'from the 5th century to the first century BC' without saying 'BC' for the 5th century; I kept the wording.
The article says 'Tambapaṇṇiya' school and gives 'Mahavihārin' interpretation; I used only the first.
The 'Calcutta-Bairat edict' is described in the article as listing works the king found advantageous; I wrote 'an edict' in the event.
Left out: Kham Pali's reasons, the Chinese Canon's printing dates, Taisho details, online editions.
